hints: Compare what happens when $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ each lose $\text{H}^+$, and think about where the leftover negative charge can go in each anion.
Think about the p orbital with the lone pair on oxygen in phenol and how overlap with the benzene pi system affects the $\text{O-H}$ bond and the stability of the anion formed.
walkthrough:
Picture the two dissociations side by side**
Think of acidity as how easily $\text{H}^+$ is lost. Water gives $\text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^-$, phenol gives $\text{H}^+ + \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$. In $\text{OH}^-$ the negative charge is stuck on one small oxygen atom. In the phenoxide ion there is a benzene ring right next to the oxygen that can help spread the charge.

See the lone pair joining the ring**
In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ the oxygen has a lone pair in a p orbital that can overlap with the delocalised pi electrons of the ring. That delocalisation pulls electron density away from oxygen toward the ring, which weakens and polarises the $\text{O-H}$ bond so $\text{H}^+$ is lost more easily.

Link delocalisation to anion stability**
Once $\text{H}^+$ is lost, the negative charge on $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$ is also delocalised into the ring. A more spread out, more stable conjugate base means the equilibrium $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^- + \text{H}^+$$ lies further to the right than for water, so phenol is the stronger acid.

Final answer: A lone pair in a p orbital on O is delocalised / overlaps with the delocalised pi system of the benzene ring.
This weakens the $\text{O-H}$ bond and stabilises the phenoxide ion, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$, so phenol dissociates more than water.

hints: Recall how strongly the $\text{-OH}$ group activates the benzene ring and how many 2,4,6 positions are available for substitution when $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ is in excess.
walkthrough:
Remember why phenol needs no catalyst**
The $\text{-OH}$ group pushes electron density into the ring so strongly that phenol reacts with bromine water instantly at room temperature, unlike benzene which needs $\text{FeBr}_3$. With excess $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ substitution happens at all available activated positions, that is positions 2, 4 and 6. That gives the white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol plus $\text{HBr}$ formed from each substitution.

hints: With dilute $\text{HNO}_3(aq)$ at room temperature phenol undergoes mono substitution only, check that $M_r$ 139 fits one $\text{NO}_2$ replacing one H, and recall which ring positions the $\text{-OH}$ group directs to.
walkthrough:
Work out what $M_r = 139$ tells you**
Phenol, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, has $M_r = 94$. Replacing one H ($A_r = 1$) by one $\text{NO}_2$ ($M_r = 46$) gives $94 - 1 + 46 = 139$. So these are mononitration products, one $\text{NO}_2$ group added.

Place the nitro group where OH directs**
The $\text{-OH}$ group is 2,4 directing and strongly activating. At room temperature with aqueous $\text{HNO}_3$ you get substitution ortho and para to $\text{OH}$, not meta. So draw a benzene with $\text{OH}$ at the top, then in one box put $\text{NO}_2$ para to it at the bottom for 4-nitrophenol, and in the other box put $\text{NO}_2$ ortho to it at the side for 2-nitrophenol.

Final answer: Two structures: benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at position 1 and $\text{NO}_2$ at position 4 (4-nitrophenol) and benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at position 1 and $\text{NO}_2$ at position 2 (2-nitrophenol).

hints: Treat phenol here like a typical acid towards an active metal, the acidic $\text{OH}$ proton is replaced by $\text{Na}$ and a gas is released.
walkthrough:
Balance the acid metal pattern**
The phenolic $\text{OH}$ behaves as the acidic proton. Sodium replaces that H to give sodium phenoxide, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa}$, and hydrogen gas bubbles off. You need two phenol molecules to make one $\text{H}_2$ molecule, so balance as $$2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2$$

hints: Recall the standard way to convert an aromatic amine $\text{-NH}_2$ into a diazonium salt $\text{-N}_2^+$ and why that first mixture must be kept very cold.
Think about what happens when a benzenediazonium salt is warmed in water alone, which small gas molecule is lost and which group replaces it to give phenol.
walkthrough:
Make the diazonium intermediate cold**
Phenylamine, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$, is first diazotised. Mix sodium nitrite with hydrochloric acid to generate nitrous acid, $\text{HNO}_2$, in the flask. Keep the temperature at or below $10 ^\circ\text{C}$, ideally in ice, because the benzenediazonium chloride, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$, decomposes if warm.

Hydrolyse warm to get phenol**
Then warm the diazonium solution with water. Heating hydrolyses the $\text{-N}_2^+$ group, nitrogen gas is evolved and $\text{-OH}$ replaces it: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{N}_2 + \text{H}^+$$ So step two needs $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ as reagent with warming above $10 ^\circ\text{C}$.

Final answer: step one reagents: $\text{NaNO}_2$ + $\text{HCl}$ (to make $\text{HNO}_2$ in situ); conditions: $T \leqslant 10 ^\circ\text{C}$, typically 0 to $5 ^\circ\text{C}$
step two reagents: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$; conditions: warm / heat, $T > 10 ^\circ\text{C}$
